question:
Select the option that corrects the following sentence.
All tickets of the FIFA World Cup have been sold away.
option_1: All tickets of the FIFA World Cup have been sold into.
option_2: All tickets of the FIFA World Cup have been sold across.
option_3: All tickets of the FIFA World Cup have been sold out.
option_4: All tickets of the FIFA World Cup have been sold among.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 3 i.e. All tickets of the FIFA World Cup have been sold out.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The phrasal verb "sell out" means to sell the entire stock of something so that none is left.
◦ Example: The concert tickets sold out within an hour of going on sale.

• In the given sentence, the context is that no tickets remain available — all of them have been sold — so the correct phrasal verb is "sold out", not "sold into/across/among", which are not standard collocations with "sell" in this sense.

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 3.

Additional Information

• Option 1: "sold into" is incorrect; "sell into" is not an established phrasal verb collocation for exhausting stock (it is sometimes used loosely for "sold into slavery/bondage", an unrelated sense).

• Option 2: "sold across" is incorrect; "across" indicates spatial extent (e.g., "sold across the country") and does not convey that stock has been exhausted.

• Option 4: "sold among" is incorrect; "among" indicates distribution amongst a group, not exhaustion of stock.

NOTE

• Other common phrasal verbs with "sell" tested in SSC exams: sell off (to sell goods, often at a reduced price, to get rid of them), sell up (to sell one's business/property entirely), and sell out (used figuratively to mean betraying one's principles for money, e.g., "He sold out to the corporation").

• Always check whether a phrasal verb collocates naturally with the given context — prepositions like "into", "across" and "among" cannot simply be swapped in for "out" without changing or destroying the intended meaning.

question:
The following sentence has been split into four segments. Identify the segment that contains a grammatical error.
The soldiers / were selected / on the section / of 'gallantry of spirits'.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 3 i.e. on the section.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The error lies in the phrase "on the section". When we mean that someone was selected/rewarded on the basis of, or because of, some quality such as gallantry, the correct preposition-based expression is "on the ground(s) of" or "on account of", not "on the section of".

• Rule: Certain nouns take a fixed preposition when expressing "reason/basis". "Ground(s)" collocates with "of" to mean "reason/basis" (e.g., "selected on the grounds of merit"); "section" is used for a division of a document, organisation, or a legal clause, and does not collocate with "of" to mean "basis/reason".

• Corrected sentence: The soldiers were selected on the grounds of 'gallantry of spirits'.

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 3.

Additional Information

• Option 1: "were selected" is grammatically correct — a correct passive-voice verb phrase (were + past participle) agreeing with the plural subject "soldiers".

• Option 2: "The soldiers" is grammatically correct — a simple plural subject with the correct definite article.

• Option 4: "of 'gallantry of spirits'." is grammatically correct as printed — it is simply the object of the (wrongly chosen) preposition phrase in segment 3; the fault lies in segment 3, not here.

NOTE

• Common confusable pairs tested in SSC error-spotting: on the ground(s) of vs. on the section of; on account of vs. because of (both correct, but "because of" is followed directly by a noun/noun phrase, never by "that").

• Other frequently tested "selected/awarded on ___ of" expressions: on the basis of, on the strength of, on the score of.

question:
The following sentence has been split into four segments. Identify the segment that contains a grammatical error.
We has travelled / to many states / of India to get / an essence of its diversity.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 4 i.e. We has travelled.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The error is a Subject-Verb Agreement error. The subject "We" is a plural (first person plural) pronoun, so it must take the plural auxiliary verb "have", not the singular "has".

• Rule — Subject-Verb Agreement: Plural subjects (We/You/They/plural nouns) take have; singular subjects (He/She/It/singular nouns) take has, in the Present Perfect tense.

• Corrected sentence: We have travelled to many states of India to get an essence of its diversity.

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 4.

Additional Information

• Option 1: "to many states" is grammatically correct — a correct prepositional phrase indicating destination.

• Option 2: "of India to get" is grammatically correct — correctly links "states" to their location "India" and introduces the infinitive of purpose "to get".

• Option 3: "an essence of its diversity" is grammatically correct — a correct noun phrase functioning as the object of "get".

NOTE

• Common subject-verb agreement traps in SSC exams: I/We/You/They + have; He/She/It/singular noun + has; with collective nouns (team, family, jury) the verb depends on whether the group acts as a single unit (singular verb) or as individuals (plural verb).

• Remember: has is also used with a third person singular subject in Simple Present (e.g., "She has a car."), so always check both the person and number of the subject before choosing "has" or "have".

question:
Select the most appropriate option to fill in the blank.
The captain dropped the trophy while he ________the victory with his teammates.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 4 i.e. was celebrating.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The sentence describes two actions happening simultaneously in the past — one ongoing action ("celebrating the victory") that was interrupted by another shorter action ("dropped the trophy").

• Rule — Past Continuous Tense: When a longer, ongoing past action is interrupted by a shorter past action (usually introduced by "while"/"when"), the ongoing action takes the Past Continuous Tense (was/were + V-ing), and the shorter interrupting action takes the Simple Past Tense.

• Structure: Simple Past (interrupting action) + while + Subject + was/were + V-ing (ongoing action). Here, "he" is singular, so the auxiliary is "was": while he was celebrating.

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 4.

Additional Information

• Option 1: "celebrated" (Simple Past) is incorrect because it would suggest the celebrating was a completed, momentary action rather than an ongoing background action at the time the trophy was dropped.

• Option 2: "celebrates" (Simple Present) is incorrect because the whole sentence is set in the past ("dropped"), and this tense would wrongly mix present time with past time.

• Option 3: "is celebrating" (Present Continuous) is incorrect for the same reason — it refers to an action happening now, not one that was ongoing in the past.

NOTE

• The "while + Past Continuous, Simple Past" pattern is one of the most frequently tested tense structures in SSC exams — e.g., "The lights went out while we were watching the movie."

• Other common past-continuous-interruption connectors: when, as, just as.

question:
Comprehension:
In the following passage, some words have been deleted. Read the passage carefully and select the most appropriate option to fill in each blank.

For decades, humans have tried to theorise the origin and evolution of the universe. Many theories have been proposed and rejected. However, the Big Bang theory has been the most (1) ______ accepted. According to this theory, the universe began as a single point, or singularity, around 13.8 billion years ago. This singularity contained all the matter and energy that would eventually (2)______ the stars, galaxies and other structures that make up our universe today. The Big Bang theory is supported by a (3)______ of observational evidence, including the cosmic microwave background radiation, the (4)________ of light elements in the universe and the large-scale structure of the cosmos. Despite its success, the Big Bang theory is still an active area of research, with scientists seeking to better understand the earliest moments of the universe and the (5)______ of dark matter and energy.

Select the most appropriate option to fill in blank number 1.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 1 i.e. widely.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The passage states that the Big Bang theory "has been the most (1) ______ accepted" theory. The standard collocation for describing a theory/idea that is accepted by most people or most of the scientific community is "widely accepted".

• Collocation rule: "Widely" combines with verbs like accepted, known, used, believed, recognised to indicate that something applies across a broad range of people/places — e.g., "a widely accepted fact", "a widely used method".

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 1.

Additional Information

• Option 2: "vastly" is incorrect; "vastly" collocates with words expressing degree/scale, such as "vastly different" or "vastly superior", not with "accepted".

• Option 3: "largely" is incorrect; "largely" means "mostly/for the most part" and is used with verbs like "depends", "due to", or "unknown" (e.g., "largely unknown"), not naturally with "accepted" in this collocational sense.

• Option 4: "loosely" is incorrect; "loosely" means "in a way that is not exact or strict" (e.g., "loosely based on"), which contradicts the sense of the theory being firmly and broadly accepted.

NOTE

• Other frequently tested collocations with "widely": widely regarded as, widely reported, widely available, widely spoken.

• In cloze passages, always check which adverb naturally pairs with the verb/adjective that follows the blank, rather than choosing based on general meaning alone.

Despite its success, the Big Bang theory is still an active area of research, with scientists seeking to better understand the earliest moments of the universe and the (5)______ of dark matter and energy.

Select the most appropriate option to fill in blank number 2.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 1 i.e. form.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The passage explains that the matter and energy in the singularity would eventually **(2)______ the stars, galaxies and other structures that make up the universe. The verb that correctly expresses matter coming together to create/constitute something new is "form"**.

• Usage rule: "Form" as a verb means to come into existence as, or to bring into existence, a particular shape/structure/entity — e.g., "Clouds form when water vapour condenses"; "The delegates will form a committee."

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 1.

Additional Information

• Option 2: "design" is incorrect; "design" implies a deliberate, planned creation by an intelligent agent, which does not fit the natural, physical process described.

• Option 3: "prepare" is incorrect; "prepare" means to make something ready for use, which does not fit the sense of matter naturally coalescing into stars and galaxies.

• Option 4: "destroy" is incorrect; it is the opposite of what the passage describes — the matter and energy create the stars and galaxies, not destroy them.

NOTE

• "Form" is commonly tested in science-based cloze passages with the sense of "to come together to create/constitute" — e.g., "Several small islands form an archipelago."

• Related word forms to remember: formation (noun, e.g., "star formation"), formative (adjective).

question:
Comprehension:
In the following passage, some words have been deleted. Read the passage carefully and select the most appropriate option to fill in each blank.

For decades, humans have tried to theorise the origin and evolution of the universe. Many theories have been proposed and rejected. However, the Big Bang theory has been the most (1) ______ accepted. According to this theory, the universe began as a single point, or singularity, around 13.8 billion years ago. This singularity contained all the matter and energy that would eventually (2)______ the stars, galaxies and other structures that make up our universe today. The Big Bang theory is supported by a (3)______ of observational evidence, including the cosmic microwave background radiation, the (4)________ of light elements in the universe and the large-scale structure of the cosmos. Despite its success, the Big Bang theory is still an active area of research, with scientists seeking to better understand the earliest moments of the universe and the (5)______ of dark matter and energy.

Select the most appropriate option to fill in blank number 3.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 2 i.e. wealth.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The passage states that the Big Bang theory "is supported by a (3)______ of observational evidence". The fixed expression "a wealth of" means a large amount of something, especially useful or valuable information/evidence/experience.

• Idiomatic collocation rule: "A wealth of" is commonly followed by abstract nouns such as evidence, information, experience, knowledge, detail — e.g., "The report is based on a wealth of data."

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 2.

Additional Information

• Option 1: "rich" is incorrect; while "rich" can mean "abundant" (e.g., "rich in evidence"), it does not fit the structure "a ______ of observational evidence" the way "wealth" does — "a rich of evidence" is not grammatical.

• Option 3: "debt" is incorrect; "debt" means money owed, which is unrelated to the amount of supporting evidence.

• Option 4: "store" is incorrect; although "a store of" can mean "a supply of", it collocates more naturally with tangible/physical or emotional reserves (e.g., "a store of energy", "a store of goodwill") rather than "observational evidence" in this formal scientific register, and is not the best fit compared to the idiomatic "a wealth of".

NOTE

• Other "a ___ of" quantity expressions frequently tested: a wealth of (a large amount, positive), a dearth of (a lack of), a plethora of (an excessive amount), a spate of (a sudden series, usually negative, e.g., "a spate of accidents").

In the following passage, some words have been deleted. Read the passage carefully and select the most appropriate option to fill in each blank.

For decades, humans have tried to theorise the origin and evolution of the universe. Many theories have been proposed and rejected. However, the Big Bang theory has been the most (1) ______ accepted. According to this theory, the universe began as a single point, or singularity, around 13.8 billion years ago. This singularity contained all the matter and energy that would eventually (2)______ the stars, galaxies and other structures that make up our universe today. The Big Bang theory is supported by a (3)______ of observational evidence, including the cosmic microwave background radiation, the (4)________ of light elements in the universe and the large-scale structure of the cosmos. Despite its success, the Big Bang theory is still an active area of research, with scientists seeking to better understand the earliest moments of the universe and the (5)______ of dark matter and energy.

Select the most appropriate option to fill in blank number 4.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 1 i.e. abundance.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The passage refers to "the (4)________ of light elements in the universe" as one of the pieces of observational evidence for the Big Bang theory. In cosmology, this specifically refers to the measured quantity/proportion of light elements (like hydrogen and helium) — the standard scientific term for this is "abundance".

• Usage rule: "Abundance" is the standard noun used in scientific writing to denote the relative quantity or proportion of a substance present — e.g., "the abundance of oxygen in the atmosphere".

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 1.

Additional Information

• Option 2: "plenty" is incorrect; "plenty" is generally used informally/predicatively (e.g., "there is plenty of evidence") and is not the standard scientific term for a measured proportion of elements.

• Option 3: "fortune" is incorrect; "fortune" refers to luck or wealth/money, which is unrelated to the measured quantity of light elements.

• Option 4: "success" is incorrect; "success" means achieving a desired result, which does not fit the sense of "quantity of light elements observed".

NOTE

• "Abundance" is a key term in science-based reading passages (chemistry, cosmology, ecology) — e.g., "natural abundance of an isotope", "relative abundance of species".

• Related word forms: abundant (adjective, e.g., "abundant evidence"), abundantly (adverb).

In the following passage, some words have been deleted. Read the passage carefully and select the most appropriate option to fill in each blank.

For decades, humans have tried to theorise the origin and evolution of the universe. Many theories have been proposed and rejected. However, the Big Bang theory has been the most (1) ______ accepted. According to this theory, the universe began as a single point, or singularity, around 13.8 billion years ago. This singularity contained all the matter and energy that would eventually (2)______ the stars, galaxies and other structures that make up our universe today. The Big Bang theory is supported by a (3)______ of observational evidence, including the cosmic microwave background radiation, the (4)________ of light elements in the universe and the large-scale structure of the cosmos. Despite its success, the Big Bang theory is still an active area of research, with scientists seeking to better understand the earliest moments of the universe and the (5)______ of dark matter and energy.

Select the most appropriate option to fill in blank number 5.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 1 i.e. nature.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The passage states that scientists are seeking to understand "the (5)______ of dark matter and energy". The correct word here is "nature", meaning the basic or inherent character/qualities of something — i.e., scientists want to know what dark matter and energy fundamentally are.

• Usage rule: "The nature of ___" is a standard formal expression used to refer to the essential character or qualities of a phenomenon, especially in academic/scientific writing — e.g., "the nature of light", "the nature of consciousness".

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 1.

Additional Information

• Option 2: "environment" is incorrect; "environment" refers to surroundings/conditions, which is unrelated to understanding what dark matter and energy fundamentally are.

• Option 3: "capture" is incorrect; "capture" means to seize or record something, which does not fit the sense of understanding the essential character of dark matter and energy.

• Option 4: "brand" is incorrect; "brand" refers to a commercial identity/trademark, which is entirely unrelated to the scientific context.

NOTE

• "The nature of" is a frequently tested formal expression in cloze passages dealing with abstract/scientific topics — contrast with "the scope of" (the extent/range of something) and "the origin of" (the source/beginning of something), both of which are also commonly tested.

question:
Select the most appropriate option that can substitute the underlined word segment in the following sentence.
The girl which is wearing a blue shirt is my sister.
option_1: which is wearing the blue shirt
option_2: who is wearing a blue shirt
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 2 i.e. who is wearing a blue shirt.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The relative pronoun "which" is used for animals and things, never for persons. Since "the girl" is a person, the correct relative pronoun is "who".

• Rule — Relative Pronouns: Who/whom is used for persons; which is used for animals and things; that can be used for both persons and things (mainly in restrictive/defining clauses).

• The verb must also agree with the singular subject "the girl", so the singular auxiliary "is" is required: who is wearing.

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 2.

Additional Information

• Option 1: "which is wearing the blue shirt" is incorrect because it retains "which" for a person; only the article has been changed, not the faulty relative pronoun.

• Option 3: "which wear a blue shirt" is incorrect for two reasons — "which" wrongly refers to a person, and "wear" does not agree with the singular subject "the girl" (should be "wears" if used at all).

• Option 4: "who wear a blue shirt" correctly uses "who" for the person but wrongly uses the plural verb "wear" instead of the singular "is wearing"/"wears" required to agree with "the girl".

NOTE

• Common relative pronoun errors tested in SSC: using "which" for people, using "who" for things/animals, and dropping subject-verb agreement after the relative pronoun.

• whose is used to show possession for both persons and things (e.g., "the girl whose bag was lost"); that is preferred over "who/which" in restrictive clauses, especially after superlatives and words like "all", "only", "the very".

question:
Select the most appropriate meaning of the underlined idiom.
The United Nations is working to eliminate the vicious cycle of poverty.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 2 i.e. One problem causes other.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The idiom "vicious cycle" means a sequence of events or conditions in which one problem causes another, which in turn worsens or reproduces the first problem, so that the situation continues or deteriorates without an easy way out. (एक समस्या से दूसरी समस्या उत्पन्न होने का दुष्चक्र)
◦ Example: Poverty leads to poor education, which leads to unemployment, which in turn leads back to poverty — a vicious cycle.

• The word "vicious" here does not mean "cruel" in the everyday sense but refers to a self-perpetuating, harmful chain of cause and effect.

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 2.

Additional Information

• Option 1: "The barrier of poverty" (गरीबी की बाधा): Incorrect — a "barrier" is a single obstacle, not a repeating chain of cause and effect.

• Option 3: "Loophole of something" (किसी चीज़ की खामी): Incorrect — a loophole is a gap or ambiguity that allows something to be avoided (e.g., a legal loophole), unrelated to a repeating cycle of problems.

• Option 4: "Strength of something" (किसी चीज़ की ताकत): Incorrect — this refers to power or robustness, the opposite sense of a harmful, self-reinforcing problem.

NOTE

• The opposite concept is a "virtuous cycle", where one positive event leads to another, producing a self-reinforcing beneficial effect.

• Other commonly tested idioms with "cycle/circle": vicious circle (same meaning as vicious cycle), come full circle (to return to the original position/situation after a series of events).

question: Select the INCORRECTLY spelt word.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 1 i.e. Innoculate.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The correct spelling is "Inoculate" — with a single "n" — meaning to introduce a vaccine or antigenic substance into the body to produce immunity to a disease.
◦ Example: Children are inoculated against measles at an early age.

• Spelling key: IN + OCULATE (one "n", one "c"). The word comes from Latin inoculare ("to graft"), and the prefix here is simply in-, not the doubled "inn-" seen in unrelated words like "innovate" or "inn".

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 1.

Additional Information

• Option 2: "Irreverent" is spelt correctly — meaning showing a lack of respect for people or things that are generally taken seriously.

• Option 3: "Immense" is spelt correctly — meaning extremely large or great.

• Option 4: "Immaculate" is spelt correctly — meaning perfectly clean, neat, or without any flaws.

NOTE

• Many candidates wrongly double the "n" in "inoculate" by confusing it with words like innovate, innate, or inn, which genuinely have a double "n".

• Other commonly confused single/double-letter spellings in SSC exams: occurrence (double c, double r), harass (single r, double s), embarrass (double r, double s), necessary (single c, double s).

question:
Identify the most appropriate ANTONYM of the underlined word in the given sentence.
The vendor said that the apples were of superior quality.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 4 i.e. Inferior.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The underlined word "superior" means of higher quality, rank, or status than others; better. (उत्कृष्ट/श्रेष्ठ)
◦ Example: This fabric is superior to the one we bought last time.

• The antonym of "superior" is "inferior", meaning of lower quality, rank, or status; worse. (निम्न कोटि का/घटिया)
◦ Example: The inferior quality of the product led to many customer complaints.

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 4.

Additional Information

• Option 1: "Excellent" (उत्कृष्ट): Incorrect — this is a near-synonym of "superior" (both mean "of very high quality"), not its opposite.

• Option 2: "Distasteful" (अरुचिकर): Incorrect — this means "unpleasant or offensive", which describes taste/behaviour, not quality ranking, and is not a direct antonym of "superior".

• Option 3: "Small" (छोटा): Incorrect — this refers to size, not quality; "superior" refers to quality/rank, so its antonym must also relate to quality/rank.

NOTE

• "Superior" and "inferior" are a classic antonym pair frequently tested in SSC exams, often alongside related pairs: superiority ↔ inferiority (nouns).

• Other quality-related antonym pairs commonly asked: premium ↔ substandard, top-notch ↔ mediocre, first-rate ↔ second-rate.

question:
Select the most appropriate synonym of the given word.
Permit
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 3 i.e. Approve.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The word "Permit" means to allow or authorise something to happen or be done. (अनुमति देना)
◦ Example: Smoking is not permitted inside the office premises.

• Its closest synonym among the options is "Approve", which means to officially agree to or accept something as satisfactory; to sanction. (स्वीकृति देना/मंजूर करना)
◦ Example: The committee approved the new construction plan.

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 3.

Additional Information

• Option 1: "Disgrace" (अपमान): Incorrect — means "loss of reputation or respect", the opposite sense of granting permission.

• Option 2: "Flout" (उल्लंघन करना): Incorrect — means "to openly disregard a rule or convention", nearly opposite to "permit".

• Option 4: "Abandon" (त्यागना): Incorrect — means "to give up or desert something completely", unrelated to granting permission.

NOTE

• Other synonyms of "permit" commonly tested: allow, authorise, sanction, license, consent to.

• Do not confuse "permit" (to allow) with "prohibit"/"forbid" (to disallow), which are its antonyms.

question:
Select the most appropriate meaning of the given idiom.
Bag and baggage
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 3 i.e. With all goods.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The idiom "Bag and baggage" means with all one's belongings/possessions; completely, leaving nothing behind. (अपना सारा सामान लेकर/पूरी तरह से)
◦ Example: The tenants were asked to vacate the house, bag and baggage, by the end of the month.

• The phrase originally referred to soldiers leaving a camp with all their equipment and personal effects, and is now used generally for moving out completely with everything one owns.

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 3.

Additional Information

• Option 1: "At the service" (सेवा में): Incorrect — this means "ready to help/assist someone", unrelated to carrying one's belongings.

• Option 2: "By force" (बलपूर्वक): Incorrect — this means "using physical strength or coercion", which is not the sense of this idiom.

• Option 4: "Fair and honest" (निष्पक्ष और ईमानदार): Incorrect — this describes honesty/impartiality, unrelated to the idiom's meaning of moving with all one's possessions.

NOTE

• Other idioms of completeness often asked in SSC: "Lock, stock and barrel" (entirely, completely), "Root and branch" (thoroughly, completely).

• Idioms involving "bag": "In the bag" (certain to be achieved/won), "Let the cat out of the bag" (to reveal a secret accidentally).

question:
Select the most appropriate homophone to fill in the blank.
Arun knows perfectly well how to mix the food items with __________.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 1 i.e. sauce.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• A homophone is a word that is pronounced the same as (or very similarly to) another word but has a different spelling and meaning. Here, "sauce" and "source" form the homophone pair being tested, along with the near-sounding "saws" and the misspelt "sause".

• "Sauce" means a thick liquid, often savoury, that is served with food to add flavour, and fits the meaning of the sentence — Arun is mixing food items with a sauce.

• Spelling key: S-A-U-C-E. Note the "au" vowel combination and the silent final "e".

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 1.

Additional Information

• Option 2: "saws" is incorrect; "saws" is the plural of "saw" (a cutting tool) or the third-person singular of the verb "to saw" — it makes no sense to "mix food items with saws".

• Option 3: "sause" is incorrect; this is simply a misspelling of "sauce" and is not a standard English word.

• Option 4: "source" is incorrect in this context; "source" means "the place or origin from which something comes" (e.g., "a source of income"), which does not fit "mixing food items with ___".

NOTE

• Commonly tested homophone pairs in SSC exams: sauce/source, their/there/they're, stationary/stationery, principal/principle, complement/compliment, desert/dessert.

• Always substitute each option back into the sentence and check for contextual meaning, not just similarity of sound.

question:
Select the most appropriate ANTONYM of the underlined word.
No one trusts her as her reasons are always explicit.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 2 i.e. Ambiguous.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The underlined word "explicit" means clearly stated, leaving no room for confusion or doubt. (स्पष्ट)
◦ Example: The instructions were explicit, so no one had any confusion.

• The antonym of "explicit" is "ambiguous", meaning open to more than one interpretation; not clearly stated or defined; vague. (अस्पष्ट/द्विअर्थी)
◦ Example: His ambiguous answer left everyone confused about his real intentions.

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 2.

Additional Information

• Option 1: "Precise" (सटीक): Incorrect — this is a near-synonym of "explicit" (both convey clarity/exactness), not its opposite.

• Option 3: "Exact" (सटीक/यथार्थ): Incorrect — this also means "accurate/precise", again a synonym rather than an antonym of "explicit".

• Option 4: "Distant" (दूर का): Incorrect — this refers to physical or emotional remoteness, unrelated to clarity of expression.

NOTE

• Note the logic of the sentence itself: "No one trusts her as her reasons are always ___" — since the reason for not trusting her should be that her reasons are unclear, the blank must mean "unclear/vague", confirming "ambiguous".

• Other synonym pairs for "explicit": clear, unambiguous, direct, plain; other synonyms for "ambiguous": vague, equivocal, obscure, unclear.

question:
Read the sentence carefully and select the most appropriate option to substitute the underlined part.
The clamour distracted the priest and made him angry.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 1 i.e. loud and confused noise.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The underlined word "clamour" means a loud, confused noise, especially caused by a crowd of people shouting. (शोर-शराबा/कोलाहल)
◦ Example: The clamour of the protesting crowd could be heard from a mile away.

• In the sentence, it is this loud, confused noise that distracts and angers the priest, which matches Option 1 exactly.

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 1.

Additional Information

• Option 2: "narrow-mindedness" (संकीर्ण सोच): Incorrect — this refers to an unwillingness to consider new ideas, unrelated to noise.

• Option 3: "introduction of new things" (नई चीज़ों का परिचय): Incorrect — this describes innovation, unrelated to the meaning of "clamour".

• Option 4: "humorous deception" (हास्यपूर्ण छल): Incorrect — this describes a funny trick or prank, unrelated to loud noise.

NOTE

• Related words: clamorous (adjective, e.g., "a clamorous crowd"), clamour (verb) meaning "to shout loudly and insistently" (e.g., "the fans clamoured for an encore").

• Other synonyms for "clamour": din, uproar, racket, commotion, hullabaloo.

question:
Select the most appropriate ANTONYM of the underlined word in the given sentence.
Essays must be concise.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 2 i.e. Lengthy.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The underlined word "concise" means giving a lot of information clearly and in a few words; brief and to the point. (संक्षिप्त)
◦ Example: The manager asked for a concise summary of the report.

• The antonym of "concise" is "lengthy", meaning very long, especially in a way that feels excessive or tedious. (लंबा/विस्तृत)
◦ Example: The lengthy speech bored most of the audience.

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 2.

Additional Information

• Option 1: "Excise" (उत्सर्जित करना/कर): Incorrect — as a verb it means "to remove/cut out", and as a noun it refers to a type of tax; neither is the opposite of "concise".

• Option 3: "Precise" (सटीक): Incorrect — this is a near-synonym of "concise" (both suggest exactness/clarity), not its opposite.

• Option 4: "Total" (कुल): Incorrect — this means "complete/entire in amount", unrelated to length or brevity of expression.

NOTE

• Other synonym pairs for "concise": brief, succinct, terse, compact, pithy; antonym pairs: concise ↔ verbose/lengthy/wordy.

• Be careful not to confuse "concise" (brief) with "precise" (exact) — they often appear together as distractors in SSC vocabulary questions.

question:
Select the most appropriate option to fill in the blank.
Which _________ do you usually take to reach your office?
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 2 i.e. route.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• "Route" means a way or course taken to get from a starting point to a destination, which fits the context of travelling to the office.
◦ Example: The bus takes a different route during peak hours.

• This question tests a set of near-homophones — route, root, rout, rude — that are frequently confused because of their similar pronunciation/spelling but have entirely different meanings.

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 2.

Additional Information

• Option 1: "rude" is incorrect; it means "impolite/discourteous", unrelated to a path taken to reach a destination.

• Option 3: "root" is incorrect; it refers to the part of a plant below the ground, or the origin/source of something (e.g., "the root cause"), not a travel path.

• Option 4: "rout" is incorrect; it means "a decisive/overwhelming defeat", unrelated to the context of travelling.

NOTE

• Commonly confused word sets in SSC exams: route/root/rout, quiet/quite/quit, later/latter, loose/lose.

• Memory tip: "route" is about travel (think of "en route"), while "root" is about plants/origins, and "rout" is about defeat.

question:
Select the correct collocation to complete the following sentence.
He made _________ use of the opportunity to travel.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 1 i.e. full.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The fixed collocation is "make full use of", meaning to use something to the greatest possible extent; to utilise something completely.
◦ Example: She made full use of the scholarship to study abroad.

• Collocation rule: "Full" is the conventional collocate with "use" in this fixed expression; English collocations are often idiomatic and cannot always be predicted by meaning alone — native usage has fixed "full use of", not "total/entire/whole use of".

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 1.

Additional Information

• Option 2: "total" is incorrect; while "total" means "complete", it does not collocate naturally with "use of" in standard English (we say "total control", "total silence", but not "total use").

• Option 3: "entire" is incorrect; "entire" typically modifies a noun directly to mean the whole of it (e.g., "the entire day"), and does not collocate with "use of" in this fixed sense.

• Option 4: "whole" is incorrect for the same reason; "whole" collocates with nouns like "day", "life", "world" (e.g., "the whole day"), but not idiomatically with "use of".

NOTE

• Other fixed collocations with "make": make good use of, make the most of, make a difference, make an effort, make progress.

• Collocations must be memorised as fixed word-partnerships since substituting a near-synonym (total/entire/whole for full) often produces an unnatural or incorrect expression, even though the individual meanings are similar.

question:
The following sentence has been split into four segments. Identify the segment that contains a spelling error.
The make-up room was filled / with incadescent lights / which added to the misery / of those subjected to make-up.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 2 i.e. with incadescent lights.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The correct spelling is "incandescent", not "incadescent" — meaning emitting light as a result of being heated; brilliantly glowing.
◦ Example: The room was lit by an incandescent bulb.

• Spelling key: IN + CAN + DES + CENT. Note the letter "n" after "ca", which is missing in the misspelt form "incadescent". The word derives from Latin incandescere, "to become white with heat".

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 2.

Additional Information

• Option 1: "which added to the misery" is spelt correctly.

• Option 3: "of those subjected to make-up" is spelt correctly.

• Option 4: "The make-up room was filled" is spelt correctly.

NOTE

• Related words to remember: incandescence (noun), incandescently (adverb).

• Commonly misspelt "-escent"/"-escence" words in SSC exams: incandescent, adolescent, luminescent, convalescence — always check for the often-dropped letters in the middle of such words.

question:
Select the most appropriate synonym of the given word.
Tedious
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 2 i.e. Boring.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The word "Tedious" means too long, slow, or dull; tiresome or monotonous. (उबाऊ/नीरस)
◦ Example: Filling out the tax forms was a tedious task.

• Its closest synonym among the options is "Boring", meaning not interesting; causing weariness or a lack of interest. (उबाऊ)
◦ Example: The lecture was so boring that half the class fell asleep.

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 2.

Additional Information

• Option 1: "Exciting" (रोमांचक): Incorrect — this is an antonym of "tedious", meaning "causing great enthusiasm or interest".

• Option 3: "Working" (कार्यरत): Incorrect — this simply means "functioning/in operation" or "engaged in a job", unrelated to dullness.

• Option 4: "Happening" (घटित होना/चर्चित): Incorrect — this means either "taking place" or, informally, "lively/fashionable", the opposite sense of "tedious".

NOTE

• Other synonyms of "tedious": monotonous, dull, tiresome, wearisome, humdrum.

• Antonyms of "tedious": exciting, interesting, engaging, stimulating — useful to know since SSC often sets both synonym and antonym questions on the same base word.

question:
Select the most appropriate option that can substitute the underlined segment in the given sentence.
Employers in many developing countries report that a lack of skilled workers is a major and increasing bottleneck for their operations, affected their capacity to innovate.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 4 i.e. affecting their capacity.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The underlined segment "affected their capacity" is grammatically wrong because a finite past-tense verb ("affected") cannot simply be tacked onto the end of the main clause after a comma without a connector.

• Rule — Present Participle Clause: When a comma is followed by a phrase that adds a further consequence/result to the main clause (without a coordinating conjunction), the verb must take the -ing (present participle) form, not a finite verb. Here, the participial phrase "affecting their capacity to innovate" correctly describes a continuing consequence of the bottleneck.

• Also note the correct verb choice: "affect" (verb, meaning "to influence") is required here, not "effect" (usually a noun meaning "result", or rarely a verb meaning "to bring about/cause").

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 4.

Additional Information

• Option 1: "affect their capacity" is incorrect; a bare present-tense verb form cannot follow a comma in this position without a subject or conjunction — it does not form a grammatical participial phrase.

• Option 2: "effecting their capacity" is incorrect; although "-ing" form is used, "effect" here is the wrong word — "to effect" means "to bring something about/cause it to happen" (e.g., "effect a change"), which does not fit "capacity to innovate" being influenced.

• Option 3: "effect their capacity" is incorrect for the same reason as above — wrong word choice ("effect" instead of "affect") and also lacks the required "-ing" form.

NOTE

• Affect vs. Effect: "Affect" is (almost always) a verb meaning "to influence" (e.g., "The rain affected the match"); "Effect" is (usually) a noun meaning "a result" (e.g., "the effect of the rain"), though it can rarely be a formal verb meaning "to cause/bring about" (e.g., "effect a change in policy").

• A comma followed by an "-ing" participial phrase describing a consequence of the main clause is a very common SSC error-correction/sentence-improvement pattern — always check whether the phrase after the comma needs a participle rather than a finite verb.

question:
Select the most appropriate option that can substitute the underlined word in the given sentence.
The dedicated teacher laboured assiduously to aid her pupils in achieving success.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 2 i.e. committed.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The underlined word "dedicated" means devoted to a task or purpose; showing loyalty or commitment. (समर्पित)
◦ Example: She is a dedicated volunteer who works every weekend at the shelter.

• Its closest synonym among the options is "committed", meaning devoted to an activity, cause, or job; showing dedication. (प्रतिबद्ध)
◦ Example: He is a committed employee who always meets his deadlines.

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 2.

Additional Information

• Option 1: "un-biased" (निष्पक्ष): Incorrect — this means "not favouring one side over another; impartial", which is a different quality from being devoted to one's work.

• Option 3: "uninvolved" (अलिप्त): Incorrect — this means "not taking part in or connected with something", nearly the opposite sense of "dedicated".

• Option 4: "apathetic" (उदासीन): Incorrect — this means "showing no interest, enthusiasm, or concern", directly opposite to the meaning of "dedicated".

NOTE

• Other synonyms for "dedicated": devoted, diligent, conscientious, earnest, hard-working.

• Antonyms of "dedicated" (useful for related antonym questions): indifferent, apathetic, half-hearted, negligent.
